title: The Jesus Prayer
hookLine: loved by Eastern Catholic and Orthodox Christians: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me
last: NOW LET YOUR SERVANT GO IN PEACE.

cards: Russia, the 1800s. A man with a knapsack walks from town to town. He heard a line from Saint Paul read in church, pray without ceasing, and it won't leave him alone.
How can anyone pray without stopping? You have to eat. You have to sleep.

He asks priest after priest. Finally an old monk hands him one short sentence and tells him to say it, and keep saying it, until it says itself. That's the story in a small anonymous book called The Way of a Pilgrim.
Nobody knows who wrote it. But the sentence is real, and very old.

teach.b: Here it is, in its common form: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Many add, a sinner. That's the Jesus Prayer.

First, the words. They're stitched out of the Gospels. A blind beggar named Bartimaeus sits by the road outside Jericho, hears Jesus passing, and shouts, in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus son of David, have mercy on me."
People tell him to be quiet. He shouts louder. In another story, a tax collector stands at the back of the Temple and won't even lift his eyes: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner."
The Jesus Prayer is those two voices, joined. Second, the name.
At its center is the name of Jesus itself.

teach.h: ONE HALF IN, ONE HALF OUT.
teach.b: For the Christians who pray it, calling the name is already a way of standing in his presence. Third, the breath.

teach.h: EAST AND WEST BOTH PRAY IT.
teach.b: Monks in the Christian East, especially on Mount Athos in Greece, learned to pray it slowly with the breath: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, breathing in; have mercy on me, breathing out.
Their way of stillness is called hesychasm, from a Greek word for quiet. Fourth, who prays it.
It's most loved by Orthodox Christians and by Eastern Catholics of the Byzantine tradition, such as Ukrainian and Melkite Greek Catholics.
The Catechism of the Catholic Church describes and commends it too, so Latin Catholics pray it as well.

teach.h: LORD JESUS CHRIST, SON OF GOD, HAVE MERCY ON ME.
teach.b: And have mercy doesn't mean cringing. It's the cry of Kyrie eleison at Mass: be kind to me, hold me, heal me.

how: Orthodox Christians and Byzantine-rite Eastern Catholics often pray the Jesus Prayer many times over on a knotted prayer rope, silently and in rhythm with the breath, and many Latin Catholics use it as well.

o: a monks' way of inner stillness, praying with the breath
a vow of total silence some monks take for life
a Greek chant sung slowly by a monastery choir

games.q: where the prayer comes from — tap the pairs.
p: be merciful to me a sinner
from a Greek word for quiet

s: only Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer
Byzantine-rite Eastern Catholics love it too, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church commends it.
its words are stitched from Gospel stories
the blind man Bartimaeus and the tax collector in the Temple.
it's the cry of Kyrie eleison: be kind to me, heal me.

games.q: you're Bartimaeus, blind by the road, and Jesus is passing. you shout for mercy, and the crowd tells you to be quiet. what do you do?
o: go quiet and wait for another day.
ask someone else to call him for you.
games.why: he cries out all the more, and Jesus stops and calls him over. his cry became half of the Jesus Prayer.

practice: Breathe it ten times, no hurry: if you pray, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God on the breath in, have mercy on me on the breath out. If your mind wanders, just start the next one.
If you don't pray, breathe in and out on one word, mercy, and notice what it does to your shoulders.

wordCard.voice: Hesychasm. The way of stillness monks on Mount Athos learned, praying the Jesus Prayer slowly in rhythm with their breath. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: have mercy on me. the same verb as Kyrie eleison, and the end of the Jesus Prayer in Greek.

carryVoice: Your line: with every breath. A prayer this short fits inside any wait. See you tomorrow.
